questions.stem: The IUPAC name of $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CHCHO}$ is
questions.explanation: The longest chain that contains the CHO carbon has three carbon atoms, so the parent name is propanal. The CHO carbon is numbered 1, which puts the methyl branch on carbon 2, giving 2-methylpropanal. This is the branched isomer of butanal, with the same molecular formula $\mathrm{C_4H_8O}$.

optionRationale.2: The aldehyde carbon is always numbered C-1, so the methyl group is on C-2, not C-3.
optionRationale.3: The longest chain has only three carbons, so the parent is propanal, not butanal.
optionRationale.4: Butanal is the straight-chain isomer; this compound has a branched chain with a methyl group.

questions.objective: Name a branched aldehyde by IUPAC rules

questions.stem: Dry distillation of calcium ethanoate (calcium acetate) gives
questions.explanation: When the calcium salt of a carboxylic acid is heated, the two acyl groups join and calcium carbonate is lost: $\mathrm{(CH_3COO)_2Ca \xrightarrow{\Delta} CH_3COCH_3 + CaCO_3}$. Two ethanoate units give propanone, a ketone, whereas a mixture of calcium ethanoate and calcium formate would instead give ethanal.

optionRationale.1: Ethanal would need calcium ethanoate and calcium formate together, not calcium ethanoate alone.
optionRationale.2: Propanal is not formed; the two ethanoate groups combine to give a ketone with three carbons.
optionRationale.3: Ethanoic acid is the parent acid and is not the product of heating its calcium salt.

questions.objective: Recall the preparation of ketones by dry distillation of calcium salts

questions.stem: The number of $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds in a molecule of propanone, $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$, is respectively
questions.explanation: The six C-H bonds, two C-C bonds and the sigma bond of the C=O group give $6+2+1 = 9$ sigma bonds. The carbonyl double bond adds one $\pi$ bond, formed by sideways overlap of $p$ orbitals on carbon and oxygen. Hence propanone has 9 $\sigma$ and 1 $\pi$ bond.

optionRationale.2: Propanone has only one C=O double bond and no other multiple bonds, so only one $\pi$ bond.
optionRationale.3: Counting gives six C-H, two C-C and one C-O sigma bonds, which is 9 and not 10.
optionRationale.4: The sigma count is correct but there is only one pi bond, in the carbonyl group.

questions.objective: Count sigma and pi bonds in a carbonyl compound

questions.stem: Ethanal is reduced with sodium borohydride, $\mathrm{NaBH_4}$, in ethanol. The product is
questions.explanation: Sodium borohydride is a mild hydride donor that adds $\mathrm{H^-}$ to the carbonyl carbon of aldehydes and ketones and, after protonation, gives alcohols. Ethanal being an aldehyde gives a primary alcohol, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}$ (ethanol). The C=O group is reduced but the carbon skeleton is unchanged.

optionRationale.1: Complete removal of the oxygen requires Clemmensen or Wolff-Kishner reduction, not NaBH$_4$.
optionRationale.3: Ethanoic acid is an oxidation product, whereas NaBH$_4$ is a reducing agent.
optionRationale.4: Ethene would form by dehydration of ethanol, which does not occur under these conditions.

questions.objective: Predict the product of reduction of an aldehyde with NaBH4

questions.stem: Which reagent converts ethanoic acid into ethanoyl chloride so that the by-products are gases, which leave the mixture and leave the product easy to purify?
questions.explanation: Thionyl chloride reacts as $\mathrm{CH_3COOH + SOCl_2 \to CH_3COCl + SO_2 + HCl}$. Both sulphur dioxide and hydrogen chloride are gases and escape, leaving pure ethanoyl chloride. With phosphorus pentachloride and phosphorus trichloride the by-products are POCl$_3$ and H$_3$PO$_3$, which are harder to remove.

optionRationale.1: It forms liquid POCl$_3$ as a by-product, which has to be separated by distillation.
optionRationale.2: It leaves phosphorous acid, H$_3$PO$_3$, a non-volatile by-product.
optionRationale.4: Chlorine substitutes at the alpha carbon, or in the alkyl group, and does not replace the OH of the acid.

questions.objective: Select the best reagent to prepare acyl chlorides from carboxylic acids

questions.stem: Match the compound in List-I with its common name in List-II.
questions.explanation: HCHO is methanal, commonly called formaldehyde. $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$ is propanone, known as acetone. HCOOH is methanoic acid, the formic acid first isolated from ants, and $\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}$ is benzenecarboxylic acid, called benzoic acid, so the match is A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.

optionRationale.1: Formaldehyde and formic acid are interchanged; HCHO is the aldehyde and HCOOH is the acid.
optionRationale.2: Acetone and formic acid are interchanged; acetone is the ketone $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$.
optionRationale.3: Every pair is incorrect; HCHO is formaldehyde, not acetone.

questions.objective: Match carbonyl compounds with their common names

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about uses of carbonyl compounds.
A. Propanone is used as a solvent, for example in nail polish remover.
B. Benzaldehyde is used in perfumery and in dye industries.
C. Sodium benzoate is used as a food preservative.
D. Propanone is a gas at room temperature.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Propanone is a volatile liquid with a boiling point near 329 K, widely used as a solvent for paints, lacquers and nail polish. Benzaldehyde has an almond-like smell and is used in perfumes and dyes, and sodium benzoate is a common preservative. Statement D is wrong because only methanal is a gas at room temperature among the common carbonyls.

optionRationale.1: D is wrong: propanone boils at about 329 K and is a liquid; C, which is correct, is missing.
optionRationale.2: It contains D, which is false, and omits A, which is true.
optionRationale.4: D is false, and the true statements B and C are left out.

questions.objective: Recall uses and physical state of common carbonyl compounds

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Aldehydes and ketones have lower boiling points than alcohols of comparable molar mass.
Reason (R): Alcohol molecules are associated through intermolecular hydrogen bonding, whereas pure aldehyde and ketone molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Both functional groups are polar, but only alcohols have an O-H bond that can form hydrogen bonds between their own molecules. Association by hydrogen bonding raises the boiling point of alcohols, whereas aldehydes and ketones are held only by weaker dipole-dipole forces. The reason is therefore the correct explanation of the assertion.

optionRationale.2: (R) is the direct cause of the boiling point difference, so it is more than a true but unrelated statement.
optionRationale.3: (R) is true: alcohols associate through O-H...O hydrogen bonds.
optionRationale.4: (A) is true: aldehydes and ketones boil lower than alcohols of similar molar mass.

questions.objective: Judge an assertion and its reason on aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids

questions.stem: Excess Tollens' reagent is added to $2.2$ g of ethanal (molar mass 44 g mol$^{-1}$). The mass of silver deposited, taking 2 mol of Ag per mole of aldehyde, is (Ag = 108 g mol$^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: Moles of ethanal $= 2.2/44 = 0.050$ mol. Each CHO group is oxidised to COO$^-$ with two electrons, which reduce two $\mathrm{Ag^+}$ ions, so Ag formed $= 2\times0.050 = 0.100$ mol. The mass is $0.100\times108 = 10.8$ g, deposited as the silver mirror.

optionRationale.1: This assumes one silver atom per ethanal, but each aldehyde group transfers two electrons and gives two Ag.
optionRationale.2: This assumes four silver atoms per ethanal; the ratio is 2 Ag for each CHO group.
optionRationale.3: This is just the mass of ethanal and ignores the stoichiometry and the molar mass of silver.

questions.objective: Calculate the mass of silver deposited in the Tollens test

questions.stem: Propanone is treated with a dilute solution of barium hydroxide. The main product is
questions.explanation: Propanone has $\alpha$-hydrogens, so with dilute base it undergoes aldol addition: the enolate of one molecule adds to the carbonyl carbon of another. The product of two propanone molecules is $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C(OH)CH_2COCH_3}$, called diacetone alcohol, 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one.

optionRationale.1: This is formed only on heating the aldol product, which loses water; it is not the product at ordinary temperature.
optionRationale.3: This would require a reducing agent, not a base.
optionRationale.4: This is a tertiary alcohol formed by Grignard addition, not by base-catalysed aldol addition.

questions.objective: Predict the aldol addition product of a ketone

questions.stem: Ethanal is treated with methylmagnesium bromide in dry ether and the product is then hydrolysed with dilute acid. The compound formed is
questions.explanation: The nucleophilic $\mathrm{CH_3^-}$ of the Grignard reagent attacks the carbonyl carbon of ethanal, giving the alkoxide $\mathrm{CH_3CH(CH_3)OMgBr}$. Hydrolysis then gives $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_3}$, propan-2-ol. All aldehydes except methanal give secondary alcohols this way, whereas methanal gives a primary alcohol and ketones give tertiary alcohols.

optionRationale.1: The carbon from the Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon, so the OH ends up on the middle carbon, not at the end.
optionRationale.2: A tertiary alcohol forms from a ketone and a Grignard reagent, but ethanal is an aldehyde.
optionRationale.3: Ethanol has only two carbons, but the new C-C bond formed by the methyl group of the Grignard reagent gives a three-carbon product.

questions.objective: Predict the alcohol formed from an aldehyde and a Grignard reagent

questions.stem: Which of these substituted benzoic acids has the lowest pKa value?
questions.explanation: The acidity of a benzoic acid depends on how well the carboxylate ion is stabilised. The nitro group withdraws electrons by both the $-I$ and $-M$ effects, spreading the negative charge of the carboxylate and making 4-nitrobenzoic acid the strongest acid of the four. Electron-releasing groups such as methyl and methoxy lower the acid strength.

optionRationale.1: The unsubstituted acid is weaker than the one carrying a strong electron-withdrawing group.
optionRationale.3: The methyl group donates electrons and destabilises the carboxylate, making it a weaker acid than benzoic acid.
optionRationale.4: The methoxy group releases electrons by resonance, so the acid is weaker than benzoic acid.

questions.objective: Compare acidities of substituted benzoic acids

questions.stem: Sodium ethanoate is heated with soda lime ($\mathrm{NaOH + CaO}$). The hydrocarbon formed is
questions.explanation: Heating the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid with soda lime removes the carboxylate carbon as sodium carbonate: $\mathrm{CH_3COONa + NaOH \xrightarrow{CaO,\,\Delta} CH_4 + Na_2CO_3}$. The product is an alkane with one carbon atom less than the acid, which is methane here.

optionRationale.1: Ethane is formed in Kolbe electrolysis, where two ethanoate ions join; soda lime removes the carboxyl carbon.
optionRationale.2: No dehydration or elimination step is involved.
optionRationale.4: Propane would need an extra carbon atom; decarboxylation lowers the chain by one.

questions.objective: Predict the product of decarboxylation of a carboxylate salt

questions.stem: A concentrated aqueous solution of sodium ethanoate is electrolysed (Kolbe electrolysis). The hydrocarbon liberated at the anode is
questions.explanation: At the anode ethanoate ions lose an electron and carbon dioxide to give methyl radicals, $\mathrm{CH_3COO^- \to CH_3\cdot + CO_2 + e^-}$. Two methyl radicals combine to give ethane. The product has twice the number of carbon atoms of the alkyl group, and hydrogen is formed at the cathode.

optionRationale.1: Methane forms by heating with soda lime, not by electrolysis.
optionRationale.2: Butane would result from the coupling of propanoate ions, not ethanoate.
optionRationale.4: Ethene is not formed; the radicals simply couple to give the alkane.

questions.objective: Predict the product of Kolbe electrolysis

questions.stem: The $K_a$ of ethanoic acid is $1.8\times10^{-5}$. The pH of its $0.10$ M aqueous solution is closest to
questions.explanation: For a weak acid, $[\mathrm{H^+}] = \sqrt{K_a c} = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-5}\times0.10} = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-6}} = 1.34\times10^{-3}$ M. Therefore pH $= -\log(1.34\times10^{-3}) = 2.87$. This is much higher than 1 because the ionisation is only about 1.3 percent.

optionRationale.1: This treats the acid as strong, giving $[\mathrm{H^+}] = 0.10$ M; ethanoic acid is only slightly ionised.
optionRationale.2: This is the $pK_a$ and applies only when the acid and its conjugate base have equal concentrations.
optionRationale.4: This gives $-\log(K_ac)$ and forgets to take the square root.

questions.objective: Calculate the pH of a carboxylic acid solution

questions.stem: $6.0$ g of ethanoic acid (molar mass 60 g mol$^{-1}$) is heated with excess ethanol and a little concentrated $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$. If the yield is 60 percent, the mass of ethyl ethanoate (molar mass 88 g mol$^{-1}$) obtained is
questions.explanation: Moles of ethanoic acid $= 6.0/60 = 0.10$ mol, and the 1:1 esterification would give 0.10 mol of ester, which is $0.10\times88 = 8.80$ g. At 60 percent yield the mass is $0.60\times8.80 = 5.28$ g. The reaction is reversible, which is why the yield is below 100 percent.

optionRationale.2: This is the theoretical yield, which ignores the 60 percent yield.
optionRationale.3: This applies 60 percent to the mass of the acid and ignores the change in molar mass.
optionRationale.4: This corresponds to a 50 percent yield, not 60 percent.

questions.objective: Calculate the yield of an esterification reaction

questions.stem: Which test can be used to distinguish pentan-2-one from pentan-3-one?
questions.explanation: Pentan-2-one, $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2CH_2CH_3}$, contains the $\mathrm{CH_3CO-}$ group and gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform with $\mathrm{I_2/NaOH}$. Pentan-3-one, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COCH_2CH_3}$, has no methyl ketone group, so it does not. The other tests respond in the same way to both ketones.

optionRationale.1: Neither compound is an aldehyde, so both give a negative result with Tollens' reagent.
optionRationale.3: Both are ketones and neither reduces Fehling's solution.
optionRationale.4: Both ketones give an orange-yellow precipitate, so the test does not distinguish them.

questions.objective: Distinguish methyl ketones from other ketones by the iodoform test

questions.stem: An alkyl cyanide is reduced with stannous chloride and hydrochloric acid, and the product is then hydrolysed with water. The final product is
questions.explanation: This is the Stephen reaction: $\mathrm{RCN + SnCl_2 + HCl \to RCH{=}NH}$ (an imine, as its salt) and then $\mathrm{RCH{=}NH \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} RCHO}$. The nitrile is reduced only as far as the imine stage and hydrolysis converts the imine to an aldehyde with the same number of carbon atoms as the nitrile.

optionRationale.1: A primary amine would result from stronger reduction, such as with LiAlH$_4$ or H$_2$/Ni.
optionRationale.3: The acid would form on direct acid hydrolysis of the nitrile, not by this partial reduction.
optionRationale.4: A ketone would need an extra alkyl group, as from a Grignard reagent, which is not involved here.

questions.objective: Recall the Stephen reaction

questions.stem: Benzene reacts with carbon monoxide and hydrogen chloride in the presence of anhydrous $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ and a little $\mathrm{CuCl}$. The product is
questions.explanation: This is the Gattermann-Koch reaction. CO and HCl with $\mathrm{AlCl_3/CuCl}$ generate the formyl cation, $\mathrm{HCO^+}$, which attacks the benzene ring in electrophilic substitution: $\mathrm{C_6H_6 + CO + HCl \to C_6H_5CHO}$. It is a direct way of introducing the CHO group into an aromatic ring.

optionRationale.1: The acid would require further oxidation, which does not happen under these conditions.
optionRationale.2: Acetophenone forms from benzene with ethanoyl chloride and AlCl$_3$ (Friedel-Crafts acylation).
optionRationale.3: An alcohol is not formed; the electrophile is the formyl cation, giving an aldehyde.

questions.objective: Recall the Gattermann-Koch formylation

questions.stem: Match the compound in List-I with its physical property in List-II.
questions.explanation: Methanal boils at about 252 K and is a gas at room temperature. Propanone is a liquid that mixes with water in all proportions because of hydrogen bonding with water. Benzoic acid is a white solid only sparingly soluble in cold water, and pure ethanoic acid freezes at about 290 K, called glacial acetic acid.

optionRationale.1: Methanal and propanone are interchanged; propanone is a liquid and methanal is the gas.
optionRationale.3: Benzoic acid and ethanoic acid are interchanged; benzoic acid is the solid and ethanoic acid is the one that freezes near 290 K.
optionRationale.4: None of these pairs is correct; for example methanal boils far below room temperature.

questions.objective: Match carbonyl compounds with their physical properties

right: I. Solid, only sparingly soluble in cold water
II. Pure acid freezes at about 290 K (glacial form)
IV. Liquid miscible with water in all proportions

questions.stem: Propanone is treated with HCN to give a cyanohydrin, which is then hydrolysed with dilute acid. The final product is
questions.explanation: HCN adds across the C=O group: $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C=O + HCN \to (CH_3)_2C(OH)CN}$, the cyanohydrin. Acid hydrolysis converts $\mathrm{-CN}$ to $\mathrm{-COOH}$ and leaves the OH untouched, giving $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C(OH)COOH}$, 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanoic acid, an $\alpha$-hydroxy acid with one more carbon atom than the ketone.

optionRationale.2: The product keeps both methyl groups of propanone on the carbon that carries the OH, so it is branched and is not a straight-chain butanoic acid.
optionRationale.3: The hydroxyl group of the cyanohydrin remains on the carbon during hydrolysis; it is not lost.
optionRationale.4: The cyanide adds to the carbonyl carbon, so OH and COOH end up on the same carbon, not on C-3.

questions.objective: Predict the product of hydrolysis of a cyanohydrin

questions.stem: $0.59$ g of a dicarboxylic acid is exactly neutralised by $10.0$ mL of $1.00$ M NaOH. The acid is (molar masses in g mol$^{-1}$: ethanedioic 90, propanedioic 104, butanedioic 118, pentanedioic 132)
questions.explanation: Moles of NaOH $= 0.0100\ \mathrm{L}\times1.00 = 0.0100$ mol. A dicarboxylic acid has two acidic groups, so moles of acid $= 0.0100/2 = 0.00500$ mol. Molar mass $= 0.59/0.00500 = 118$ g mol$^{-1}$, which matches butanedioic acid, $\mathrm{HOOC(CH_2)_2COOH}$.

optionRationale.1: Its molar mass is 90, so 0.59 g would be 0.0066 mol and would need 13.1 mL of the alkali.
optionRationale.2: Its molar mass is 104, so 0.59 g would need 11.3 mL of 1.00 M NaOH.
optionRationale.3: Its molar mass is 132, so 0.59 g would need only 8.9 mL of 1.00 M NaOH.

questions.objective: Identify a dicarboxylic acid by titration

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Ethanal gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent.
Reason (R): Ethanal contains $\alpha$-hydrogen atoms.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Ethanal reduces Tollens' reagent because its CHO group is easily oxidised to a carboxylate, which reduces $\mathrm{Ag^+}$ to silver. Ethanal does contain three $\alpha$-hydrogens, but these are responsible for aldol condensation and the iodoform reaction, not for reducing Tollens' reagent, so (R) is true but not the explanation.

optionRationale.1: (R) is true but the silver mirror arises from the aldehydic CHO group, not from the alpha-hydrogens, so it is not the explanation.
optionRationale.3: (R) is true; ethanal has three alpha-hydrogens, so it cannot be called false.
optionRationale.4: (A) is true: ethanal gives the silver mirror with Tollens' reagent.

questions.objective: Judge an assertion and its reason on aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Benzoic acid does not undergo Friedel-Crafts alkylation.
Reason (R): The carboxyl group is an activating group in electrophilic aromatic substitution.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The carboxyl group withdraws electrons from the ring by the $-I$ and $-M$ effects, so the ring is deactivated towards electrophiles, and the acid also forms a complex with the $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ catalyst. Friedel-Crafts reactions therefore fail with benzoic acid. The assertion is true; the reason says the group is activating, which is false.

optionRationale.1: (R) is false: the carboxyl group deactivates the ring, so it cannot explain (A).
optionRationale.2: (R) is not a true statement, so the option saying it is true but not explanatory is wrong.
optionRationale.4: (A) is true: benzoic acid does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reactions.

questions.objective: Judge an assertion and its reason on aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Aldehydes and ketones undergo electrophilic addition at the carbonyl group.
Reason (R): The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic because the C=O bond is polarised towards oxygen.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the carbonyl carbon carries a partial positive charge and is attacked by nucleophiles. The characteristic reaction is therefore nucleophilic addition, not electrophilic addition. The reason correctly describes the polarity of the group, but the assertion has the wrong type of reaction.

optionRationale.1: (A) is false, since the typical reaction is nucleophilic addition, so the pair cannot be explained.
optionRationale.2: (A) is not true; carbonyl compounds do not undergo electrophilic addition.
optionRationale.3: (R) is true: the C=O bond is polarised towards oxygen, so it is not a false reason.

questions.objective: Judge an assertion and its reason on aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements.
A. Carboxylic acids are reduced to primary alcohols by lithium aluminium hydride.
B. The Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction gives $\alpha$-halocarboxylic acids.
C. The esterification of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol is irreversible.
D. Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones in nucleophilic addition reactions.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: LiAlH$_4$ is a strong reducing agent that reduces $\mathrm{RCOOH}$ to $\mathrm{RCH_2OH}$. The HVZ reaction (Br$_2$ with red phosphorus) halogenates at the $\alpha$-carbon. Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones owing to less steric hindrance and a more positive carbonyl carbon. Esterification is reversible, so C is false.

optionRationale.1: C is wrong: esterification reaches an equilibrium and can be reversed by hydrolysis; D, which is true, is missing.
optionRationale.2: It contains the wrong statement C and omits A.
optionRationale.3: It contains C, which is wrong, and omits the correct statement B.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on reactions of carboxylic acids and carbonyl compounds

questions.stem: A compound X, $\mathrm{C_4H_8O}$, gives a yellow precipitate with $\mathrm{I_2/NaOH}$ and does not reduce Tollens' reagent. On Wolff-Kishner reduction it gives butane. X is
questions.explanation: The iodoform result shows a methyl ketone group, and a negative Tollens' test excludes an aldehyde. Wolff-Kishner reduction converts $\mathrm{C=O}$ to $\mathrm{CH_2}$, and giving butane shows an unbranched four-carbon skeleton. Therefore X is $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2CH_3}$, butan-2-one.

optionRationale.2: Butanal reduces Tollens' reagent and cannot give iodoform because it lacks the methyl ketone group.
optionRationale.3: It is an aldehyde, gives the silver mirror test, and reduction would give isobutane rather than butane.
optionRationale.4: It has the formula $\mathrm{C_4H_8O}$ but contains no carbonyl group, so Wolff-Kishner reduction and the iodoform test do not apply.

questions.objective: Identify a carbonyl compound from chemical tests

questions.stem: A buffer solution contains $0.20$ M ethanoic acid and $0.10$ M sodium ethanoate. Given $pK_a = 4.76$ for ethanoic acid, the pH of the buffer is
questions.explanation: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is $\mathrm{pH} = pK_a + \log\dfrac{[\mathrm{salt}]}{[\mathrm{acid}]}$. Substituting, $\mathrm{pH} = 4.76 + \log(0.10/0.20) = 4.76 + \log0.5 = 4.76 - 0.30 = 4.46$. The acid is in excess, so the pH is below the $pK_a$.

optionRationale.2: The ratio of base to acid is inverted; salt is the numerator in the Henderson equation.
optionRationale.3: The pH equals the $pK_a$ only when the acid and salt concentrations are equal.
optionRationale.4: The log term has been counted twice; $\log(0.5) = -0.30$ is subtracted just once.

questions.objective: Calculate the pH of an ethanoate buffer

questions.stem: Ethyne is hydrated with dilute $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ and $\mathrm{HgSO_4}$ to give X. X is treated with $\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}$ followed by hydrolysis to give Y, and Y is oxidised with acidified $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$ to give Z. Z is
questions.explanation: Hydration of ethyne gives the enol, which tautomerises to ethanal (X). Ethanal with $\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}$ then $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$ gives propan-2-ol (Y), a secondary alcohol. Oxidation of a secondary alcohol stops at the ketone stage, so Z is $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$, propanone.

optionRationale.1: Y is a secondary alcohol, so oxidation gives a ketone, never an aldehyde.
optionRationale.2: A secondary alcohol cannot be oxidised to a carboxylic acid with the same number of carbons.
optionRationale.4: Ethanoic acid would be the oxidation product of X, but X was first converted to Y by the Grignard step.

questions.objective: Deduce the product of a multi-step sequence from ethyne

questions.stem: Benzaldehyde is treated with $\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}$ and then hydrolysed to give X. X is oxidised with $\mathrm{CrO_3}$ to give Y. Y is warmed with $\mathrm{I_2}$ and NaOH. The products of this last step are
questions.explanation: Benzaldehyde and $\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}$ give 1-phenylethanol, $\mathrm{C_6H_5CH(OH)CH_3}$ (X). Oxidation gives acetophenone, $\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}$ (Y). Having a $\mathrm{CH_3CO-}$ group, Y gives the iodoform reaction: $\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3 + 3I_2 + 4NaOH \to C_6H_5COONa + CHI_3 + 3NaI + 3H_2O}$.

optionRationale.1: The haloform reaction gives iodoform, CHI$_3$, and not methyl iodide; the carboxylic acid is obtained as its sodium salt in alkaline solution.
optionRationale.3: Benzaldehyde is not formed; the CO-CH$_3$ group is cleaved to give the benzoate.
optionRationale.4: Y is acetophenone, which has the $\mathrm{CH_3CO-}$ group needed for a positive iodoform test.

questions.objective: Deduce the products of a multi-step sequence ending in the haloform reaction
